deck.name: HTTP Status Codes and Semantics
deck.description: Status code classes and the codes worth knowing by heart, plus HTTP method semantics and caching rules. Facts are drawn from the current HTTP specifications (RFC 9110, RFC 9111) and the extension RFCs that define the newer codes. Where a code comes from an extension or an obsolete document, the card says so.

topics.description: What the first digit tells a client.
The request appears to be at fault.
The server is aware that it failed or cannot comply.
Safe, idempotent, cacheable and what each method asks for.

notes.front: What does the first digit of an HTTP status code tell a client?
notes.back: The class of the response, grouping codes by the kind of outcome.

notes.front: Which status code class reports that a request was received and is still being handled?
notes.back: 1xx

notes.front: Which status code class reports that the request succeeded?
notes.back: 2xx

notes.front: Which status code class points the client at a different place to get the result?
notes.back: 3xx

notes.front: Which status code class blames the request itself?
notes.back: 4xx

notes.front: Which status code class blames the server?
notes.back: 5xx

notes.front: Are HTTP status codes a fixed, closed list?
notes.back: No, the registry grows, so a client must cope with a code it does not recognise by using its class.

notes.front: What does a 100 Continue response tell a client?
notes.back: That the request headers arrived and the client may send the request content.

notes.front: Which status code confirms a protocol change requested by the client?
notes.back: 101 Switching Protocols

notes.front: What is the 103 response used for?
notes.back: Sending response headers such as Link before the final response is ready, so a client can start work early.

notes.front: Which status code was defined for WebDAV to show that a long request was accepted but still running?
notes.back: 102 Processing, defined in RFC 2518 and dropped by RFC 4918.

notes.front: Do 1xx responses end an HTTP exchange?
notes.back: No, an interim response is followed by the final response for the same request.

notes.text: Responses in the {{c1::1xx}} class are interim, so the final response for the request is still to come.
notes.extra: A client may ignore an interim response it does not understand.

notes.front: What does a 200 response to a GET carry?
notes.back: The selected representation in the response content.

notes.front: Which status code tells a client that a new resource now exists?
notes.back: 201 Created, usually with a Location header naming the new resource.

notes.front: What does a 202 response mean about the work the request asked for?
notes.back: The request was accepted for processing, but the processing is not finished.

notes.front: When is 203 the appropriate status code?
notes.back: When a transforming proxy has changed the response headers received from the origin.

notes.front: What does a 204 response tell a client about the response content?
notes.back: There is none, and the client should keep showing the document it already has.

notes.front: What does a 205 response ask a client to do?
notes.back: Reset the document view that caused the request, for example by clearing a submitted form.

notes.front: What does a 206 response carry?
notes.back: The requested byte ranges of the selected representation.

notes.front: Which status code lets a client resume a large download in pieces?
notes.back: 206 Partial Content

notes.front: What does a 207 response report?
notes.back: A separate status code for each part of a WebDAV request that touched several resources.

notes.front: What problem does 208 exist to solve?
notes.back: Repeating the same WebDAV resource over and over inside a 207 response.

notes.front: What does 226 report?
notes.back: That the response is a delta against a cached representation rather than the whole thing.

notes.front: Which status code suits a successful DELETE that has nothing to report?
notes.back: 204 No Content

notes.text: A successful POST that creates a resource typically answers with {{c1::201}}, and names the new resource in the {{c2::Location}} header.
notes.extra: The Location header may also appear on 3xx responses, where it names the redirect target.

notes.front: What does a 301 response tell a client about the URL to use in future?
notes.back: The new URL in the Location header is the permanent one for that resource.

notes.front: How do the permanent redirects 301 and 308 differ?
notes.back: 301 has historically allowed a client to turn a POST into a GET, while 308 forbids any change of method.

notes.front: Which redirect status codes guarantee that the request method stays as it was?
Why does 302 have a reputation for changing the request method?
notes.back: Early clients were allowed to turn a POST into a GET when following it, which is part of why 307 and 308 were defined.

notes.front: What does a 303 response instruct a client to fetch?
notes.back: The resource named in Location, using GET, so the original request is not repeated.

notes.front: Which status code is the usual answer to a form submission that should not be re-posted on refresh?
notes.back: 303 See Other

notes.front: What does a 304 response contain?
notes.back: No content, only the headers needed to confirm that the client's stored copy is still usable.

notes.front: Which status code confirms that a cached copy may still be used?
notes.back: 304 Not Modified

notes.front: What does a 300 response indicate?
notes.back: The target has several representations and the response lists them for the client to choose from.

notes.front: Which status code is deprecated because it forced clients to use one fixed proxy?
notes.back: 305 Use Proxy

notes.front: Which status code number is reserved and carries no meaning?

notes.text: When a client follows a redirect, the new target comes from the {{c1::Location}} response header.
notes.extra: Always check where a redirect points before sending credentials to the new location.

notes.front: What does a 400 response mean?
notes.back: The server will not process the request because of a client error such as malformed syntax.

notes.front: What separates 401 from 403 in practice?
notes.back: 401 means the credentials are missing or invalid, while 403 means the server understood who is asking and refuses anyway.

notes.front: Which response header does a 401 response need?
notes.back: WWW-Authenticate, describing how to authenticate.

notes.front: What does a 403 response tell a client about repeating the request with the same credentials?
notes.back: That repeating it will change nothing, so the request should be abandoned.

notes.front: Which status code is often returned in place of 403 so that the existence of a resource stays hidden?
What does a 404 response prove about whether a resource ever existed?
notes.back: Nothing definite, because the server may be concealing a resource that is really there.

notes.front: Which status code says a resource used to exist but has been deliberately removed?
notes.back: 410 Gone

notes.front: What must accompany a 405 response?
notes.back: An Allow header listing the methods the target does support.

notes.front: What does a 406 response mean?
notes.back: The server cannot produce a representation that matches the client's Accept headers.

notes.front: What does a 407 response ask of a client?
notes.back: Authentication with the proxy, described in the Proxy-Authenticate header.

notes.front: What causes a 408 response?
notes.back: The server gave up waiting for the request that the client had begun to send.

notes.front: What does a 409 response indicate about the target resource?
notes.back: The request conflicts with the resource's current state, so the client must resolve the difference.

notes.front: Which status code fits a failed update that lost a race with another writer?
notes.back: 409 Conflict

notes.front: What does a 411 response mean?
notes.back: The request omitted a Content-Length header that the target requires.

notes.front: What does a 412 response mean?
notes.back: A precondition in the request evaluated to false on the server.

notes.front: What does a 413 response indicate?
notes.back: The request content is larger than the server is prepared to process.

notes.front: What does a 414 response indicate?
notes.back: The request target is longer than the server is prepared to interpret.

notes.front: What does a 415 response indicate?
notes.back: The content type of the request is not supported by the target resource.

notes.front: What does a 416 response report about the byte range asked for?
notes.back: That the range is unsatisfiable for the selected representation.

notes.front: What does a 417 response mean?
notes.back: The server is unable to meet the expectations listed in the Expect header.

notes.front: Which status code comes from an April Fools document and is not part of the core HTTP specification?
notes.back: 418, from RFC 2324, the teapot joke.

notes.front: What does a 421 response mean?
notes.back: The request reached a server that cannot produce a response for the target URI.

notes.front: What does a 422 response mean?
notes.back: The request was well formed but its instructions could not be carried out, which RFC 9110 renamed to Unprocessable Content.

notes.front: What does a 423 response report in WebDAV?
notes.back: That the target resource is locked.

notes.front: What does a 424 response report in WebDAV?
notes.back: That an earlier request in the same batch failed, so this one was skipped.

notes.front: What does a 425 response mean?
notes.back: The server refuses a request that might be replayed, such as one sent in early data.

notes.front: What does a 426 response ask a client to do?
notes.back: Move to another protocol, named in the Upgrade header, before retrying.

notes.front: What does a 428 response mean?
notes.back: The origin requires the request to be conditional, for example with If-Match, before it will act.

notes.front: What is a 429 response saying?
notes.back: The client sent too many requests in a given time and should slow down.

notes.front: Which response header tells a client how long to pause after a 429?
notes.back: Retry-After

notes.front: What does a 431 response mean?
notes.back: The header section of the request is larger than the server is willing to accept.

notes.front: What does a 451 response report?
notes.back: That a legal demand prevents the server from serving the resource.

notes.text: A {{c1::401}} response describes how to authenticate in the {{c2::WWW-Authenticate}} header, while a {{c3::407}} response does the same for a proxy.
notes.extra: Retrying a 403 with the same credentials achieves nothing.

notes.text: A {{c1::409}} response tells the client that the request clashes with the resource's current state.
notes.extra: Conditional requests with If-Match are the usual way to avoid that clash.

notes.text: A {{c1::405}} response must list the supported methods in the {{c2::Allow}} header.
notes.extra: The Allow header may also appear on other responses as a hint.

notes.front: What does a 500 response mean?
notes.back: The server met an unexpected condition that stopped it fulfilling the request.

notes.front: What does a 501 response mean?
notes.back: The server does not support the functionality the request needs.

notes.front: How does 504 differ from 502?
notes.back: 502 means an upstream server sent something unusable, while 504 means an upstream server sent nothing in time.

notes.front: What does a 502 response indicate?
notes.back: An intermediary received an invalid response from the server further along the chain.

notes.front: What does a 503 response indicate?
notes.back: The server is temporarily unable to handle the request, from overload or maintenance for example.

notes.front: Which status code suits planned maintenance announced with a Retry-After header?
notes.back: 503 Service Unavailable

notes.front: What does a 504 response indicate?
notes.back: An intermediary got no timely answer from the server further along the chain.

notes.front: What does a 505 response mean?
notes.back: The server does not support the major HTTP version used in the request.

notes.front: What does a 506 response report?
notes.back: An internal configuration error in the server's content negotiation.

notes.front: What does a 507 response report in WebDAV?
notes.back: The server cannot store the representation needed to complete the request.

notes.front: What does a 508 response report?
notes.back: The WebDAV server detected an endless loop while processing the request.

notes.front: What does a 510 response report?
notes.back: The server needs the request to be extended before it can fulfil it.

notes.front: What does a 511 response mean?
notes.back: The client must authenticate to get network access, as on a captive portal.

notes.front: What does a 5xx code tell a client about who should fix the problem?
notes.back: The server knows that the fault is on the server side, so the client gains nothing by changing the request.

notes.text: A {{c1::502}} comes from a gateway that received a broken reply, while a {{c2::504}} comes from a gateway that waited too long.
notes.extra: Both point at something behind the intermediary rather than at the caller.

notes.text: A {{c1::503}} response often carries a {{c2::Retry-After}} header so clients can back off politely.
notes.extra: Without that header a client has to guess when to try again.

notes.front: What does the word safe mean for an HTTP method?
notes.back: The method is defined to request no change to the server's state, so it may be repeated harmlessly.

notes.front: Which HTTP methods are defined as safe?
notes.back: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE

notes.front: Which HTTP methods are idempotent?
notes.back: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE

notes.front: What does idempotent mean for an HTTP request?
notes.back: Sending it several times has the same intended effect on the server as sending it once.

notes.front: Is POST idempotent?
notes.back: No, repeating it may create a second resource, which is why automatic retries are risky.

notes.front: Is PATCH idempotent?
notes.back: Not in general, because a patch description may be written so that applying it twice changes the result.

notes.front: What does a HEAD request return?
notes.back: The headers a GET would return, with no content, which makes it cheap for checking freshness.

notes.front: Which method asks a server to describe the communication options for a target?
notes.back: OPTIONS

notes.front: What does the TRACE method ask a server to do?
notes.back: Return the request it received, so the client can see what intermediaries changed on the way.

notes.front: Which HTTP methods may be stored by a cache without explicit instructions?
notes.back: GET and HEAD

notes.front: What does a PUT request ask a server to do with the target resource?
notes.back: Replace the state of the target with the representation supplied in the request.

notes.front: What does a PATCH request carry?
notes.back: A description of the changes to apply to the target, rather than a full replacement.

notes.front: What does a DELETE request ask for?
notes.back: Removal of the association between the target resource and its current functionality.

notes.front: Which method is neither safe nor idempotent and typically creates a subordinate resource?
notes.back: POST

notes.front: What does the CONNECT method establish?
notes.back: A tunnel to the server named in the request target.

notes.front: Which response header lists the methods a target supports?
notes.back: Allow

notes.front: Which status code should an origin server return for a method that is unrecognised or unimplemented?
notes.back: 501 Not Implemented

notes.front: Why do browsers treat a GET as safe to repeat and a POST as needing care?
notes.back: A GET is defined to change nothing on the server, while a POST may change it every time it arrives.

notes.text: A {{c1::safe}} method changes nothing on the server, and every safe method is also {{c2::idempotent}}.
notes.extra: PUT and DELETE are idempotent without being safe.

notes.text: The {{c1::PUT}} method replaces the whole representation at the target, while {{c2::PATCH}} applies a change to it.
notes.extra: Both are aimed at the state of one resource.

notes.text: The two methods that leave server state untouched are {{c1::GET}} and {{c2::HEAD}}.

notes.front: What does the max-age cache directive express?
notes.back: How many seconds a stored response stays fresh, counted from the moment it was generated.

notes.front: What does no-store instruct a cache to do?
notes.back: Keep nothing from the request or the response on disk or in memory.

notes.front: What does the private cache directive mean?
notes.back: The response belongs to one user, so a shared cache must leave it alone.

notes.front: What does no-cache require of a cache?
notes.back: That it revalidate the stored response with the origin before reusing it.

notes.front: What does must-revalidate add to a freshness rule?
notes.back: Once stale, the response may not be reused until the origin has confirmed it.

notes.front: What does stale-while-revalidate allow?
notes.back: Serving a stale response while the cache refreshes that entry in the background.

notes.front: Which directive allows a stale response when the origin is unreachable?
notes.back: stale-if-error

notes.front: What does an entity tag identify?
notes.back: One specific version of a representation of a resource.

notes.front: How do strong and weak entity tags differ?
notes.back: A strong tag must match byte for byte, while a weak tag, written with a W/ prefix, only claims semantic equivalence.

notes.front: What does a client achieve by sending If-None-Match with a GET?
notes.back: A 304 answer instead of the body when the stored version still matches.

notes.front: How does If-Match protect an update against a lost update?
notes.back: The server acts only while the entity tag still matches what the client read.

notes.front: What does the Vary header tell a cache?
notes.back: Which request headers took part in selecting the response, so the stored entry is keyed on them too.

notes.front: Which header carries the moment a response was generated at the origin?
notes.back: Date

notes.front: Which header carries how long a response has been sitting in caches?
notes.back: Age

notes.front: What is the difference between a fresh and a stale stored response?
notes.back: Fresh means its age is still within the freshness lifetime, stale means that lifetime has passed.

notes.text: A client proves it already holds a version by sending the {{c1::ETag}} back in an {{c2::If-None-Match}} header.
notes.extra: A matching tag earns a 304 response with no body.

notes.text: When a response varies by language, the cache needs the {{c1::Vary}} header to avoid handing the wrong version to the next reader.
notes.extra: A missing Vary header is a classic cause of mixed-up cached content.

notes.text: The {{c1::max-age}} directive sets the freshness lifetime in seconds, and {{c2::no-store}} forbids keeping the response at all.
notes.extra: Both may appear on a request or a response, with slightly different meanings.
